old_receipt.title: SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm

new_receipt.title: SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm

old.text: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in scientific research aims to improve agents’ research capabilities through their own experimental experience. Scientific agent swarms can pursue this goal when one agent’s findings and implementations advance another’s research. Two obstacles stand in the way. A failed experiment does not reveal whether its hypothesis or its implementation was at fault, and a program without overall gains can hide components that other agents need. We introduce SwarmRSI , a framework in which a swarm improves its research by evolving the research states its agents inherit, including hypotheses, programs and experimental evidence. Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation uses other agents’ feedback to decide whether to revise a hypothesis or its program. Complementary Swarm Recombination tests retained hypotheses on other agents’ programs and combines complementary components. Recursive Swarm Evolution returns every outcome to a shared graph that guides which state each agent updates next. SwarmRSI achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on OpenProblems and NatureBench. With Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, it reaches an average score of 76.2 on OpenProblems, and it matches the published SOTA on 44.4% of NatureBench tasks, the highest Match-SOTA rate among compared methods. On MLE-Bench Lite, it wins medals on 81.8% of tasks, above hypothesis and program evolution agents with the same backbone. With DeepSeek-V4-Pro in one seed over all 90 NatureBench tasks, about 77% of final best programs descend from a rebase, a crossover or an update triggered by feedback. Biologists reproduce two of its programs and use them in follow-up analyses of intestinal and splenic immunity.

new.text: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in scientific research aims to improve agents’ research capabilities through their own experimental experience. Scientific agent swarms can pursue this goal when one agent’s findings and implementations advance another’s research. Two obstacles stand in the way. A failed experiment does not reveal whether its hypothesis or its implementation was at fault, and a program without overall gains can hide components that other agents need. We introduce SwarmRSI , a framework in which a swarm improves its research by evolving the research states its agents inherit, including hypotheses, programs and experimental evidence. Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation uses other agents’ feedback to decide whether to revise a hypothesis or its program. Complementary Swarm Recombination tests retained hypotheses on other agents’ programs and combines complementary components. Recursive Swarm Evolution returns every outcome to a shared graph that guides which state each agent updates next. SwarmRSI achieves state-of-the-art performance across three benchmarks, scoring 76.2 on OpenProblems, attaining a 44.4% Match-SOTA rate on NatureBench, and earning medals on 81.8% of MLE-Bench Lite tasks. Across 90 NatureBench tasks, 77% of the best programs descend from feedback-guided mutation or recombination. Biologists further validate two generated programs in studies of intestinal and splenic immunity. The code is available 1 1 1 https://github.com/EvoScientist/SwarmRSI .
